questions.question: How do you deploy a Spring Boot application to Azure Spring Apps?
questions.title: Deploying Spring Boot to Azure Spring Apps
questions.direct_answer: You deploy to Azure Spring Apps using the Azure CLI or Maven plugin: provision the service instance, create an app, then deploy the JAR. Azure manages the Spring runtime, service discovery, and config server.

interviewer_intent.testing: Hands-on familiarity with Azure Spring Apps provisioning and deployment workflow.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Azure Spring Apps with a generic App Service deployment — missing the spring-specific config server and service registry features.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the managed Spring Cloud Config Server, eureka service registry, and blue-green deployment via staging deployments.

sections.title: Why a Spring-Specific PaaS Exists When App Service Already Deploys JARs
sections.content:
Deploying a Spring Boot application to a generic cloud VM or App Service means you're responsible for service discovery, configuration management, and health routing — the entire Spring Cloud infrastructure that your microservices depend on. Azure Spring Apps exists because Microsoft and VMware recognized that teams shouldn't have to operate their own Eureka cluster, Config Server, and Spring Cloud Gateway just to run a few Spring Boot services.

The platform provisions a **managed Eureka service registry** and a **managed Spring Cloud Config Server** backed by a Git repository. Your Spring Boot services register with Eureka automatically on startup and pull externalized configuration from the Config Server — without deploying or maintaining either component. This is the critical distinction from a generic App Service deployment, and the mistake most candidates make is treating Azure Spring Apps as just another PaaS for JARs. The Spring-specific managed components are the entire point.

Azure Spring Apps also provides **staging deployments** for blue-green releases. You deploy a new version to the staging slot, validate it against the staging endpoint, and swap traffic with a single CLI command. If the new version fails, you swap back — the previous production deployment is still running.

sections.title: Three Commands From Nothing to a Running Service
sections.content:
The deployment workflow has three commands: create the service instance, create an app within it, and deploy the JAR. The service instance is the container for all your apps and their shared managed infrastructure. Each app within the service maps to one deployable Spring Boot artifact.

```bash
az group create --name my-rg --location eastus

az spring create \
  --name my-spring-service \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --sku Standard

az spring app create \
  --service my-spring-service \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --name order-api \
  --runtime-version Java_17 \
  --assign-endpoint true

az spring app deploy \
  --service my-spring-service \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --name order-api \
  --artifact-path target/order-api-1.0.jar
```

The `--assign-endpoint true` flag creates a public URL for the app. In production, you'd typically leave this off and route traffic through Azure Application Gateway or Front Door instead. The `--sku Standard` tier includes the managed Config Server and Eureka — the Basic tier omits these, which removes the primary advantage of the platform.

sections.title: The Managed Spring Cloud Features That Justify the Platform
sections.content:
The managed Config Server connects to a Git repository you specify, and every app in the service instance pulls configuration from it at startup. This implements the Spring Cloud Config pattern without deploying `spring-cloud-config-server` as a separate service.

```bash
az spring config-server set \
  --service my-spring-service \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --config-file config-server-settings.json
```

The configuration file points to a Git repo with `application.yml` profiles organized by service name and environment. When your Spring Boot app starts, it resolves `spring.config.import=configserver:` automatically — the platform injects the Config Server URI. The managed Eureka registry allows your services to discover each other by application name without hardcoded URLs.

The **Enterprise tier** adds commercial VMware Tanzu components: Application Accelerator for project scaffolding, API Portal for centralized API documentation, and Application Live View for real-time actuator inspection across all deployed apps. For most teams, the Standard tier covers the essential Spring Cloud infrastructure. The Enterprise tier becomes relevant when operating dozens of services with a dedicated platform team managing the shared infrastructure.

sections.title: Zero-Downtime Releases Through Staging Deployments
sections.content:
Staging deployments are how you achieve zero-downtime releases without building your own blue-green infrastructure. Rather than deploying directly to production, you create a staging deployment, validate it, and swap.

```bash
az spring app deployment create \
  --service my-spring-service \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --app order-api \
  --name green \
  --artifact-path target/order-api-2.0.jar

curl https://my-spring-service-order-api-green.azuremicroservices.io/actuator/health

az spring app set-deployment \
  --service my-spring-service \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --name order-api \
  --deployment green
```

The first command deploys the new version as a named deployment (`green`) alongside the existing production deployment. The staging deployment gets its own URL for smoke testing. The `set-deployment` command swaps production traffic to the green deployment atomically. If something goes wrong, running `set-deployment` again with the original deployment name rolls back instantly — both deployments remain running until you explicitly delete one.

Your CI/CD pipeline should create the staging deployment, run integration tests against the staging URL, and only swap if tests pass. The swap itself is a metadata change at the platform level — no pods restart, no connections drop.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Managed Config Server and Eureka eliminate self-hosted Spring Cloud infrastructure** — Azure Spring Apps provisions these from a Git repo and service registry URL; no pods to manage, patch, or scale
- **Deploy with CLI or Maven plugin** — `az spring app deploy --artifact-path target/app.jar` deploys the JAR; `mvn azure-spring-apps:deploy` integrates with the Maven build pipeline
- **Environment variables override `application.properties`** — configure database URLs and feature flags in the portal or CLI; reference secrets via `spring-cloud-azure-starter-keyvault-secrets` to avoid plaintext in config
- **Application Insights auto-collects metrics and traces** — attach the Java agent or use the built-in integration; HTTP latency, exception rates, and dependency traces appear without SDK changes
- **Horizontal scaling with Availability Zone distribution** — `az spring app scale --instance-count N`; Azure distributes across AZs automatically; configure health checks so instances are replaced if they fail

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Azure Spring Apps (formerly Azure Spring Cloud) is a managed platform specifically designed for Spring Boot services — it provides built-in Spring Cloud infrastructure like Config Server and Service Registry without you running and maintaining those components.

**What Azure Spring Apps manages for you**
- Spring Cloud Config Server: Azure Spring Apps provisions and manages Config Server backed by a Git repository — which means your Spring Boot services pull configuration from a central Git repo without you deploying a Config Server pod
- Eureka Service Registry: Spring Boot services register and discover each other through a managed Eureka instance; you configure your application.properties with the registry URL and Azure handles the rest
- Distributed tracing: built-in Application Insights integration collects traces from every service without manual SDK configuration

**Deploying a Spring Boot application**
- Package the Spring Boot app as a JAR; deploy with the Azure CLI: `az spring app deploy --name my-service --artifact-path target/app.jar`; or use the Azure Spring Apps Maven plugin: `mvn azure-spring-apps:deploy`
- Configure environment variables and connection strings in the Azure portal or CLI — these override `application.properties` values; keep database URLs and passwords in Azure Key Vault, referenced via the Spring Cloud Azure Key Vault starter

**Scaling and monitoring**
- Azure Spring Apps scales horizontally by setting the instance count per service — `az spring app scale --name my-service --instance-count 5`; it distributes instances across Availability Zones automatically
- Application Insights is the default monitoring integration — it collects HTTP request metrics, latency distributions, dependency traces, and exceptions without any SDK changes in your application

Use Azure Spring Apps when: you're already committed to Spring Cloud patterns, want managed Config Server and Eureka, and don't need custom Kubernetes capabilities. Use AKS when you need full Kubernetes control.

questions.question: How do you build a CI/CD pipeline to deploy a Java application from Azure Container Registry to AKS?
questions.title: Azure Container Registry + AKS Deployment Pipeline
questions.direct_answer: Build the Docker image, push it to Azure Container Registry, then apply a Kubernetes deployment manifest referencing the ACR image. Use GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps Pipelines to automate the workflow.

interviewer_intent.testing: End-to-end understanding of a containerized Java deployment pipeline on Azure — from source to running Kubernetes pod.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Storing ACR credentials as plaintext secrets in the pipeline instead of using the AKS-ACR integration (az aks update --attach-acr) for credential-free pulls.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention multi-stage Docker builds to reduce image size, image vulnerability scanning with Defender for Containers, and rolling update strategy in the Deployment spec.

sections.title: Four Handoffs, Four Places to Leak Credentials or Break Deployments
sections.content:
Getting a Java application from a Git commit to a running Kubernetes pod involves four handoffs: build the application, package it as a container image, push the image to a registry, and update the Kubernetes cluster to run the new image. Each handoff is a place where teams introduce security vulnerabilities or operational fragility. The most common mistake is storing Azure Container Registry credentials as plaintext secrets in the pipeline — a practice that creates rotation overhead and a credential leak surface.

Azure's solution is the **ACR-AKS integration**: a single CLI command (`az aks update --attach-acr`) grants the AKS cluster's kubelet identity the `AcrPull` role on your registry. After this, AKS pulls images from ACR without `imagePullSecrets` in your pod specs. No registry passwords in Kubernetes secrets, no rotation schedules, no credential expiration alerts.

The second critical practice is **immutable image tags**. Tagging every image with the Git commit SHA (not `latest`) ensures that every deployment is traceable to a specific commit, rollbacks deploy a known-good image, and image vulnerability scans are attributable to a specific build. A tag of `latest` is ambiguous — it could be yesterday's build or last month's, and `kubectl rollout undo` might pull a completely different image than expected.

sections.title: ACR-AKS Integration — No Registry Passwords in Your Cluster
sections.content:
The setup is two commands: create the registry and attach it to your cluster. Under the hood, this creates an RBAC role assignment that grants the kubelet's Managed Identity pull access.

```bash
az acr create \
  --name myregistry \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --sku Standard

az aks update \
  --name my-cluster \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --attach-acr myregistry
```

The `--attach-acr` command grants the AKS cluster's kubelet managed identity the `AcrPull` role on the registry. The kubelet uses this identity to authenticate image pulls without any Kubernetes secret. This works regardless of whether ACR and AKS are in the same subscription — cross-subscription role assignments are supported.

For the CI pipeline's push access, use a service principal with the `AcrPush` role or — better — federated credentials with GitHub Actions OIDC. The `azure/login` GitHub Action supports OIDC-based authentication, eliminating long-lived credentials from your pipeline secrets entirely. This means no stored passwords anywhere in the system: AKS pulls with Managed Identity, and the pipeline pushes with OIDC-federated tokens.

sections.title: Multi-Stage Dockerfile — 800 MB Build Image to 180 MB Runtime
sections.content:
A multi-stage Dockerfile separates the build environment from the runtime, dramatically reducing the final image size and attack surface.

```dockerfile
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn dependency:go-offline -B
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn package -DskipTests -B

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/*.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

The build stage uses a full Maven image with the JDK (~800 MB), but the final image uses only the JRE on Alpine Linux (~180 MB). The `dependency:go-offline` step is cached by Docker layer caching — dependencies only re-download when `pom.xml` changes, not on every code change. This reduces build times from minutes to seconds for iterative development.

The Alpine-based JRE image also has a smaller CVE surface. Enable **Defender for Containers** on your ACR to scan every pushed image for known vulnerabilities. Configure it to block deployments of images with critical CVEs by using an Azure Policy assignment that denies pods referencing images with scan failures.

sections.title: The Pipeline Ties It Together — Fail Fast on Broken Deployments
sections.content:
The pipeline ties build, push, and deploy together. The critical details are tagging images with the Git commit SHA and using `kubectl rollout status` to make the pipeline fail if the deployment doesn't succeed.

```yaml
name: Deploy to AKS
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: azure/login@v2
        with:
          client-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
          tenant-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
      - run: |
          az acr login --name myregistry
          IMAGE=myregistry.azurecr.io/my-api:${{ github.sha }}
          docker build -t $IMAGE .
          docker push $IMAGE
      - uses: azure/aks-set-context@v3
        with:
          resource-group: my-rg
          cluster-name: my-cluster
      - run: |
          kubectl set image deployment/my-api \
            my-api=myregistry.azurecr.io/my-api:${{ github.sha }}
          kubectl rollout status deployment/my-api --timeout=300s
```

The `kubectl rollout status --timeout=300s` command blocks until the rollout succeeds or fails. Without it, the pipeline reports success immediately after updating the image reference — even if the new pods crash-loop. The Kubernetes Deployment should specify `maxUnavailable: 0` in the rolling update strategy and point the readiness probe at `/actuator/health/readiness` with `initialDelaySeconds: 15` to give the JVM time to start. If the new image fails readiness checks, the rollout stalls and the pipeline fails — catching the broken deployment before users are affected.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Git SHA as image tag enables traceability and rollback** — `myacr.azurecr.io/my-service:abc1234` links every deployed image to a commit; rollback is `kubectl set image` with an older SHA
- **ACR in the same region as AKS eliminates cross-region transfer** — AKS pulls images from ACR over the Azure backbone; no public internet bandwidth cost; image pulls are fast even for large JVM images
- **`az aks update --attach-acr` configures pull permissions** — grants the AKS Managed Identity `acrPull` on ACR; no imagePullSecrets in Kubernetes manifests; credentials managed by Azure AD
- **Helm tracks release history** — `helm upgrade` records the previous release; `helm rollback my-service 1` reverts to the previous version's manifests and image tag in one command
- **AKS rolling deployment by default** — `strategy: RollingUpdate` with `maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0` ensures old pods stay until new pods pass readiness checks; configure readiness probe on `/actuator/health/readiness`

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The Azure container deployment pipeline — build, push to ACR, deploy to AKS — follows a consistent four-stage pattern regardless of whether you use Azure DevOps Pipelines, GitHub Actions, or Jenkins.

**Build stage**
- Build the Spring Boot JAR with Maven or Gradle, then build the Docker image — a multi-stage Dockerfile builds the JAR in a JDK stage and copies the artifact to a JRE final image to minimize image size
- Use the Git commit SHA as the image tag: `docker build -t myacr.azurecr.io/my-service:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) .` — which means every deployed image is traceable to a specific commit, making rollback straightforward

**Push to ACR**
- Authenticate to ACR with `az acr login --name myacr` (development) or a service principal with `acrPush` role (CI); push the tagged image
- ACR geo-replication mirrors images to the same regions as AKS clusters — which means image pulls from AKS are fast and don't traverse the public internet; use ACR in the same region as AKS to avoid cross-region latency

**Deploy to AKS**
- Update the Kubernetes Deployment manifest with the new image tag: `kubectl set image deployment/my-service my-service=myacr.azurecr.io/my-service:SHA`
- Or use Helm: update the `image.tag` value and `helm upgrade my-service ./charts/my-service --set image.tag=SHA`; Helm tracks release history, making `helm rollback` a single command

**AKS authentication to ACR**
- Attach ACR to AKS with `az aks update --attach-acr myacr` — this grants the AKS kubelet's Managed Identity the `acrPull` role on ACR; pods pull images without imagePullSecrets or stored credentials

questions.question: How do Azure Functions work with Java, and how do they compare to a traditional Spring Boot deployment?
questions.title: Azure Functions with Java — Serverless Spring
questions.direct_answer: Azure Functions run Java code triggered by events (HTTP, timer, Service Bus, blobs). You annotate methods with @FunctionName and trigger annotations. Unlike Spring Boot, there's no embedded server — the Functions host manages the lifecycle and scales to zero.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the serverless execution model, cold starts, and when to use Functions vs. a long-running Spring Boot service.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating a Function as a Spring Boot controller — injecting Spring context into Functions adds startup overhead and complicates the cold-start problem.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Durable Functions for stateful workflows, the Premium plan for pre-warmed instances, and the azure-functions-maven-plugin for deployment.

sections.title: Why Keep a JVM Running 24/7 for a Job That Takes 200 Milliseconds?
sections.content:
Running a Spring Boot application 24/7 on App Service or AKS makes sense when the service handles continuous traffic. But some workloads are inherently event-driven: process a file when it's uploaded, react to a message on a queue, run a cleanup job every midnight. Keeping an entire JVM instance running for tasks that execute for 200 milliseconds every few minutes is wasteful — both in cost and operational overhead.

Azure Functions addresses this by managing the JVM lifecycle entirely. There's no embedded Tomcat, no `main()` method, no long-running process. You write a class with an annotated method, deploy it, and the Functions host decides when to start and stop JVM instances based on trigger activity. The Consumption plan takes this to the extreme — your function scales to zero when idle and spins up instances on demand, billing only for actual execution time.

The challenge with Java Functions is **cold start latency**. When a Consumption plan instance starts from zero, the JVM needs to initialize, load classes, and run your initialization code. For a lean function without Spring, this takes 2–3 seconds. For a function that bootstraps a Spring context with dependency injection, component scanning, and bean initialization, cold start can reach **10–15 seconds** — a deal-breaker for synchronous HTTP endpoints but acceptable for queue consumers and timer triggers.

sections.title: Functions vs Spring Boot — Different Tools for Different Workload Shapes
sections.content:
The comparison isn't about which is better — it's about which workload shape matches which execution model. A full CRUD API with complex domain logic doesn't belong in Functions; a blob trigger that resizes images doesn't need Spring Boot.

| Dimension | Azure Functions (Java) | Spring Boot on App Service |
|---|---|---|
| Lifecycle | Host manages JVM start/stop | Always running (you manage restarts) |
| Scaling | Event-driven, scale-to-zero | Rule-based autoscale, always ≥1 instance |
| Cold start | 2–15s depending on complexity | None (JVM always warm) |
| Billing | Per execution + GB-seconds | Per hour/month (fixed plan) |
| Framework | Functions annotations, no embedded server | Full Spring MVC, Tomcat/Netty |
| Best fit | Short event handlers, glue logic | Full API services, complex domain logic |
| DI support | Basic (manual wiring or Spring Cloud Function) | Full Spring context |
| Deployment | `azure-functions-maven-plugin` | JAR/WAR to App Service or container |

sections.title: Lean Functions Start in 2 Seconds — Spring Functions Take 15
Durable Functions Turn Stateless Handlers Into Workflow Orchestrators
sections.content:
**Durable Functions** extends the serverless model to handle stateful workflows — something that plain Azure Functions cannot do because each invocation is stateless. The orchestrator pattern lets you define a workflow that coordinates multiple activity functions, waits for external events, and survives host restarts.

Three patterns make Durable Functions valuable. **Fan-out/fan-in** executes multiple activity functions in parallel and aggregates their results — process 100 images concurrently, then generate a report from all results. **Human interaction** pauses the orchestration waiting for an external approval event, with a configurable timeout. **Long-running sagas** chain activities with compensating transactions — charge the card, reserve inventory, confirm shipping; if shipping fails, release inventory and refund the card.

The orchestrator achieves durability by checkpointing state to Azure Storage after each activity completes. If the host restarts or scales, the orchestration resumes from the last checkpoint. Java support for Durable Functions uses the `durabletask-azure-functions` extension, and while it's newer than the C# implementation, it supports the core patterns.

Durable Functions fills the gap between simple event handlers and full workflow engines like Azure Logic Apps or Temporal. For order processing pipelines and document approval workflows where each step takes minutes to hours, Durable Functions provides the right abstraction without requiring dedicated workflow infrastructure.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@FunctionName` + trigger annotation = one function** — `@HttpTrigger`, `@ServiceBusQueueTrigger`, `@TimerTrigger`; the runtime handles trigger subscription and delivers the event to the method
- **Input/output bindings eliminate SDK boilerplate** — `@CosmosDBOutput` writes the function result to Cosmos DB without Cosmos SDK calls; `@BlobInput` reads a blob without Storage SDK calls; bindings are declared, not coded
- **Consumption Plan: zero cost when idle; Premium: no cold starts** — Consumption bills per invocation and scales to zero; Premium keeps pre-warmed instances alive; choose based on whether latency on first request matters
- **Java cold start: 1-5 seconds on Consumption** — JVM class loading + optional Spring initialization; minimize dependencies and Spring auto-configuration for latency-sensitive HTTP functions; use GraalVM native image for sub-100ms cold start
- **`@ServiceBusQueueTrigger` provides at-least-once delivery** — function success = message completed; exception = message abandoned; configure `maxDeliveryCount` before messages move to the DLQ

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Azure Functions runs Java code triggered by events — HTTP requests, queue messages, timer schedules, blob uploads — with per-invocation billing and no infrastructure to manage.

**Function structure**
- A Java Azure Function is a class with a method annotated with `@FunctionName` and one or more binding annotations — `@HttpTrigger` for HTTP, `@ServiceBusQueueTrigger` for Service Bus, `@TimerTrigger` for scheduled execution
- Input and output bindings are declared as method parameters or return types: `@BlobInput` reads a blob when the function fires; `@CosmosDBOutput` writes results to Cosmos DB without SDK calls
- The Azure Functions runtime handles the trigger subscription and passes the event to your method; no Spring ApplicationContext is involved unless you use Spring Cloud Function

**Cold starts — the Java challenge**
- Java functions have cold starts of 1-5 seconds after periods of inactivity — the JVM initializes and loads classes before the first invocation
- Premium Plan provides pre-warmed instances that eliminate cold starts at the cost of always-on minimum compute; Consumption Plan is zero-cost when idle but has cold starts
- Using Spring Cloud Function with Azure Functions adds ApplicationContext startup time to the cold start; keep Spring configuration minimal for latency-sensitive functions

**Triggers and output bindings**
- `@ServiceBusQueueTrigger` processes messages from a Service Bus queue; the function completes successfully = message committed; throws exception = message abandoned (retry)
- `@TimerTrigger(schedule = "0 0 * * * *")` runs every hour using a CRON expression — distributed timer that runs on one instance, not all instances
- Output binding: return an object and annotate the method with `@CosmosDBOutput` to write the result to Cosmos DB without a database SDK call

Azure Functions is appropriate for: event-driven processing of Service Bus messages, S3/blob-triggered processing, scheduled batch jobs, lightweight HTTP endpoints with bursty traffic. Avoid for: long-running processes (limit: 10 min on Consumption, 60 min on Premium).

beats.text: Running a Spring Boot application 24/7 on App Service or AKS makes sense when the service handles continuous traffic. But some workloads are inherently event-driven: process a file when it's uploaded, react to a message on a queue, run a cleanup job every midnight. Keeping an entire JVM instance running for tasks that execute for 200 milliseconds every few minutes is wasteful — both in cost and operational overhead. Azure Functions addresses this by managing the JVM lifecycle entirely. There's no embedded Tomcat, no main() method, no long-running process. You write a class with an annotated method, deploy it, and the Functions host decides when to start and stop JVM instances based on trigger activity. The Consumption plan takes this.

items: Durable Functions extends the serverless model to handle stateful workflows — something that plain Azure Functions cannot do because each invocation is stateless
The orchestrator pattern lets you define a workflow that coordinates multiple activity functions, waits for external events, and survives host restarts
Three patterns make Durable Functions valuable
Fan-out/fan-in executes multiple activity functions in parallel and aggregates their results — process 100 images concurrently, then generate a report from all results
Human interaction pauses the orchestration waiting for an external approval event, with a configurable timeout
